title: Bend Contour Electron Tomography (BCET): Quantitative strain and topography mapping
authors: Henry G. Bell, Chenhang Xu, Arthur McCray, Minyong Han, Yicheng Zhuang, Harold Y. Hwang, Colin Ophus, Alfred Zong
abstract: Freestanding thin films of quantum materials naturally develop sub-micrometer, nonuniform strain fields that strongly affect their electronic, magnetic, and structural properties in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium conditions. However, current methods to quantitatively resolve these mesoscopic features are primarily restricted to scanning probes, making it challenging for dynamical measurements such as single-shot imaging and femtosecond microscopy. Here, we present a new computational framework which we denote as bend contour electron tomography (BCET), which efficiently converts bend contours in transmission electron microscope images into quantitative two-dimensional maps of strain and topography. By iteratively minimizing a designed loss function between experimental and simulated bend contour images, BCET retrieves both surface morphology and in-plane strain tensor fields without requiring scanning or diffraction mapping. We applied BCET to freestanding SrTiO$_3$ thin films, demonstrating the successful reconstruction of the local strain distribution and curvature field with high fidelity. Our approach provides a quantitative framework for characterizing mesoscale structures in freestanding films using wide-field imaging, opening new avenues to investigate how spatial inhomogeneity governs phase transitions and nonequilibrium dynamics in two-dimensional quantum materials.
summary: This work introduces Bend Contour Electron Tomography (BCET), a novel computational framework to quantitatively map strain and topography in freestanding quantum thin films using wide-field TEM images. By treating the analysis as an inverse problem, BCET reconstructs strain and surface geometry without requiring scanning probes. This opens new avenues for studying how spatial strain inhomogeneity governs phase transitions in 2D quantum materials.
main_problem: The challenge is to quantitatively map sub-micrometer, nonuniform strain fields and topography in freestanding quantum thin films, especially for fast, dynamical measurements.
main_result: The authors developed BCET, a framework that successfully reconstructs local strain distributions and curvature fields in $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ films using wide-field TEM imaging.
method: BCET treats the problem as a physics-constrained inverse problem, iteratively minimizing a loss function comparing measured bend contours to simulated images derived from a parameterized surface geometry and strain tensor.
model_or_system: The study uses freestanding thin films of quantum materials, specifically $	ext{SrTiO}_3$, which naturally develop strain fields. The analysis relies on interpreting bend contours observed in transmission electron microscope images.
key_observables: Quantitative 2D maps of in-plane strain tensor fields and surface morphology (topography).
important_parameters: Sub-micrometer length scales; varying sample tilt angles ($	heta_a, 	heta_ eta$); strain tensor components.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the ability to vary sample tilt angles (tomography concept) and uses a Bézier surface mesh for parameterization, which may limit nanoscale resolution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the principles of bend contours using $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ films, showing how compressive/tensile strain regions correlate with observable contrast in simulated dark-field TEM images.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the BCET computational framework (forward model, inverse minimization), applies it to $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ films, and demonstrates the quantitative reconstruction of strain and topography.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter characterization, the use of iterative, physics-constrained inverse problem solving and multi-scale optimization techniques is highly relevant to computational physics methods applicable in quantum simulation.
